Chapter 33

The trips list and a new trip

A list awaited in markup with a failed snippet and no pending one; a preview per card through query.batch — two requests for twenty trips; a thumbnail component; and a creation form whose date picker writes hidden inputs named by the form itself, prefilled from the explore page.

By the end of this chapter

Compose a page from two remote reads and one remote form, and let a headless picker participate in a form it knows nothing about.

The boundary has a failed snippet and no pending one, for the reason the comment gives: on the server every promise inside is awaited before the HTML is sent, so the first paint is the list, and a pending snippet is what the server would render instead. Inside the loop, every card awaits tripPreview(trip.id); those calls are made in the same tick, and query.batch sends them as one request. Twenty trips is two round trips, not twenty-one. Both declarations are $derived, so a refreshed query redraws the list rather than leaving the first answer on screen. When the server refuses, the failed snippet prints error.message: it is handed an App.Error, { status, message }, the failure after handleError (chapter 14). The first version wrote error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error), and since an App.Error is a plain object the list read [object Object]. Now an end-to-end test makes the preview request invalid on its way out and expects the server’s own sentence (chapter 42). The card link uses href() from chapter 23 — resolve() with the route id, then the language prefix — so a renamed folder is a type error and not a 404. There is one link per card, named by the trip, and an ::after on it covers the whole card, so the card is the click target while the accessible name stays the name. On pointer down, or Enter, the card’s title takes view-transition-name: trip-title — the name must be unique on the page, so it goes on the one card being opened — and the trip page’s <h1> carries the same name, so the title morphs into the header during the navigation.

A new account’s trips list is empty, and so is a search that matches nothing and a trip with no expenses; all three are Empty, so “nothing here yet” looks and reads the same everywhere. Its one action is a Snippet prop — action?: Snippet, rendered with {@render action()} — because the caller knows what the action is: a link to the new-trip form here, a button that clears the search on the explore page. A snippet passed as a child, {#snippet action()}…{/snippet} inside <Empty>, *is* that prop, by name, so the call site reads like markup and the component stays ignorant of what it is rendering. The title is a paragraph in the display face, not a heading — “No expenses yet” must not be a second heading in a section already called Expenses — and the card sits at the left edge, like the heading above it, and centres its contents inside: a card floating in the middle of a left-aligned page had read as a dialog that had lost its way.

Why a snippet, and not an href and a label

An href and a label would cover the first use and not the second — a button that runs a function — and the third prop added for it (onaction?) would be the start of a component that grows an option per caller. A snippet hands the caller the whole slot: link, button, two buttons if a page ever needs them, with the caller’s own types and event handlers. The component owns the frame, the caller owns the content, and neither needs to know the other’s details.

The thumbnail is the library’s sparkline idea applied to a route: longitude across, latitude up, scaled to fit — wrong for the world and right for a trip, once a degree of longitude is shrunk by the cosine of the trip’s middle latitude, as it is on the ground. Without that, Iberia at 40°N was a flat smear across the top half of the box, drawn a third wider than it is. The route goes through every stop and the dots do not: five stops in one city are five rings drawn over each other at this size, a smudge, so a stop closer than 6 units to one already drawn shares its dot. role="img" with the trip’s name is what a screen reader gets. Chapter 41 tests it in a browser: three points, three circles, one path. The box is drawn at width × height — 160×90 on the trips list, 320×160 in the embed frame — and its shape comes from those two numbers, style:aspect-ratio, not from a fixed 16:9 in the CSS that letterboxed the embed’s 2:1 drawing between two empty bands. It is shown at whatever width the card or the frame is, so the route and the stops carry vector-effect: non-scaling-stroke — without it the 2px line would be 4px on a wide card and 1px in a narrow embed. And it holds still: twenty thumbnails tracing themselves at once would be the opposite of one thing moving at a time.

A new trip

Three things in one form. The name is prefilled from ?place=, which the explore page sets: the gazetteer comes from the prerendered places(), already in the browser’s cache from the page that linked here, and as("text", suggested) sets the initial value. The description and currency are ordinary fields. The dates are the picker from chapter 21 — and the picker renders its own hidden inputs, so they must carry the names SvelteKit expects, which encode the field’s type. So the names come from fields.startDate.as("hidden", …).name, the same call the form’s own inputs use, and the picker never learns what a remote form is. The issues for both dates are gathered into one prop and shown under the field.

This is the general pattern for any third-party input inside a remote form: let the library render what it renders, and give it the name that fields.x.as(...) would have produced. The form then receives the value the same way it would from a plain <input>, with JavaScript on or off.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain why the trips boundary has no pending snippet and how many requests twenty cards cost.
  • You can say how the picker’s hidden inputs get their names and why that matters.
  • You know how the explore page prefills the name without a store or a context.
